questions.title: Long answer 1
questions.stem: Halogen ions.

parts.prompt: What ion is formed by all members of the halogens?
parts.model: A 1- ion (an anion), such as F⁻, Cl⁻, Br⁻ or I⁻.

parts.prompt: Explain what happens to the atom as it ionizes.
parts.model: A halogen has 7 valence electrons. It gains 1 electron to complete its octet. Its protons and nucleus do not change, so the extra electron gives it a 1- charge.

questions.title: Long answer 2
questions.stem: A compound contains an unknown ion X and forms the ionic compound XCl₂. Ion X contains 10 electrons.

parts.prompt: What is the charge on X? Explain.
parts.model: 2+. Two Cl⁻ ions give 2-, so X must be 2+ for the compound to be neutral.

parts.prompt: What is the identity of element X?

questions.title: Long answer 3
questions.stem: A member of the alkali metal family whose most stable ion contains 36 electrons forms a compound with chlorine.

parts.model: Alkali metals form 1+ ions, so protons = 36 + 1 = 37: rubidium (Rb⁺).

parts.prompt: What is the correct formula for this compound?
parts.model: Rb⁺ and Cl⁻ balance one to one: RbCl.

questions.title: Long answer 4
questions.stem: An ion of Pb-297 has lost 2 electrons. (VERIFY: real lead isotopes are about Pb-204 to Pb-208, so 297 may be a typo. Use the number as given; the method is the same.)

parts.prompt: How many protons, neutrons and electrons are in the ion?
How many subatomic particles in total?

parts.model: ²⁹⁷₈₂Pb²⁺: mass number 297 on top, atomic number 82 below, charge 2+ at the upper right.

questions.title: Long answer 5
questions.stem: Calcium cyanide, Ca(CN)₂.

parts.prompt: Count the atoms of each element.
parts.model: 1 Ca, 2 C, 2 N (the 2 outside the parentheses doubles both C and N).

questions.title: Long answer 6
questions.stem: Barium bonds with phosphorus.

parts.prompt: Give the ion each element forms.
parts.model: Barium (group 2) forms Ba²⁺; phosphorus (group 15) forms P³⁻.

questions.title: Long answer 7
questions.stem: Lithium bonds with nitrogen.

parts.prompt: Give the ion each element forms.
parts.model: Lithium (group 1) forms Li⁺; nitrogen (group 15) forms N³⁻.

questions.title: Long answer 8
questions.stem: An ion with a charge of 4+ has 46 electrons and 70 neutrons.

questions.title: Long answer 9
questions.stem: Carbonic acid, H₂CO₃.

questions.title: Long answer 10
questions.stem: Explain each of the following.

parts.prompt: Why does an ionic bond form?
parts.model: A metal loses electrons to become a cation and a nonmetal gains them to become an anion, so both complete their octets. The opposite charges attract: that electrostatic force is the ionic bond.

parts.prompt: Why does the identity of an element depend on the number of protons it has?
parts.model: The number of protons is the atomic number, which sets the element. Electrons can be gained or lost (ions) and neutrons can vary (isotopes), but changing the protons makes a different element.

parts.prompt: Why is atomic mass on the periodic table a decimal?
parts.model: Elements exist as a mixture of isotopes. The table lists the average of their masses, weighted by each isotope's abundance, so it is usually not a whole number.

parts.prompt: Why do elements in the same group have similar chemical behavior?
parts.model: Elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons, and chemical behavior comes from the electrons, so they bond in similar ways.

sections.name: True/False
tips: One wrong word makes a statement false. Check the particle (proton, neutron, electron) and the direction (gain or lose).

questions.stem: Metals are found to the left of the metalloid staircase.
questions.exp: Metals are left of the staircase and in the inner transition rows.

questions.stem: Hydrogen is a metal because it sits in group 1.
questions.exp: Hydrogen is a nonmetal even though it sits on the left.

questions.stem: Elements in the same period have the same number of valence electrons.
questions.exp: Same period means the same number of electron shells. Same group means the same valence electrons.

questions.stem: At room temperature (25 °C) there are 11 gaseous elements and 2 liquid elements.
questions.exp: The rest are solids.

questions.stem: The actinide series is named after the element actinium.
questions.exp: It follows actinium (Ac, 89). Your review sheet wrote "actinide" by mistake.

questions.stem: Thomson's plum pudding model placed electrons in fixed orbits around a nucleus.
questions.exp: Thomson had electrons scattered in a sphere of positive charge. Fixed orbits are Bohr's model.

questions.stem: Chadwick discovered the neutron by bombarding beryllium with alpha particles.
questions.exp: The neutral radiation was a stream of neutrons.

questions.stem: Dalton's theory says atoms are created and destroyed in chemical reactions.
questions.exp: Dalton said atoms are not created or destroyed; reactions only regroup them.

questions.stem: Almost all of an atom's mass is in its nucleus.
questions.exp: Protons and neutrons have mass; electrons are nearly massless.

questions.stem: The number of electrons determines which element an atom is.
questions.exp: The number of protons does. Electrons determine chemical behavior and charge.

questions.stem: Isotopes of an element have different chemical properties because they have different numbers of neutrons.
questions.exp: Isotopes have almost identical chemistry, because chemistry depends on electrons.

questions.stem: Carbon-13 has 7 neutrons.
A cation is formed when an atom gains electrons.
questions.exp: Gaining electrons makes an anion. A cation forms when an atom loses electrons.

questions.stem: Noble gases tend not to form ions because their valence shell is complete.
questions.exp: They already have an octet (helium has 2).

questions.stem: Ionic compounds are electrically neutral overall.
questions.exp: The charges of the cations and anions add to zero.

questions.stem: Covalent compounds form when a metal transfers electrons to a nonmetal.
questions.exp: That describes an ionic compound. Covalent compounds share electrons between nonmetals.

questions.stem: The unit of molar mass is grams per mole (g/mol).
questions.exp: Molar mass is the mass of one mole.

questions.stem: One mole of CCl₄ contains 4 moles of chlorine atoms.
questions.exp: The subscript gives the mole ratio.

why: The subscripts are crossed onto the wrong ions, so the charges do not add to zero.
The charges of these two ions are not equal in size, so one of each does not balance.

sections.name: MCQ Set A: atoms and isotopes
tips: Read every choice, then cross off the ones you can prove wrong.
For particle questions write Z, A and the charge first: p = Z, n = A - Z, e = Z - charge.
For formulas, write both ion charges before you look at the choices, then check the sum is zero.
Distractors are built from real mistakes: a skipped subscript, swapped abundances, a reversed crossover. Name the mistake behind each wrong choice.

questions.stem: A certain isotope contains 23 protons and 28 neutrons. What are its mass number and identity?
questions.exp: Mass number = protons + neutrons = 23 + 28 = 51. Atomic number 23 is vanadium (V).
why: 28 is the neutron count, not the atomic number. The element is set by the 23 protons.
23 is the atomic number. The mass number adds protons and neutrons: 23 + 28 = 51.
Antimony has 51 protons. Here 51 is the mass number; the 23 protons make it vanadium.

questions.stem: In Rutherford's experiment most alpha particles passed straight through the metal foil. What did this show?
options: Electrons are spread through positive charge
The atom is mostly empty space
Electrons orbit in fixed energy levels
questions.exp: If most particles meet nothing, most of the atom is empty space.
why: That is Thomson's plum pudding model, which this experiment disproved.
Neutrons were found later, by Chadwick in 1932. Alpha particles passing through says nothing about them.
That is Bohr's 1913 model. Particles passing through show empty space, not orbits.

questions.stem: A few alpha particles in Rutherford's experiment bounced almost straight back. What does that tell you?
options: The foil atoms are solid, packed spheres
A tiny, dense, positive center exists
Alpha particles carry a negative charge
questions.exp: Positive alpha particles were repelled by a small, dense, positive region: the nucleus.
why: Electrons are negative and nearly massless, so they attract rather than repel positive alpha particles and could not turn them back.
If atoms were solid spheres, most particles would bounce back, not just a few.
Alpha particles are positive. The bounce comes from repulsion between two positive charges.

questions.stem: Which pair of symbols shows two isotopes of the same element?
questions.exp: Isotopes share an atomic number (bottom number) and differ in mass number. Both of these have Z = 10.
why: Same mass number, but the atomic numbers differ (10 and 11), so these are different elements.
The atomic numbers differ (10 and 12), so these are different elements.
The atomic numbers differ (9 and 11), so these are different elements.

questions.stem: How many protons, neutrons and electrons are in a neutral atom of ¹³⁶₅₆Ba?
questions.exp: Protons = Z = 56; neutrons = 136 - 56 = 80; neutral, so electrons = 56.
why: 136 is the mass number. Neutrons = 136 - 56 = 80.
Protons and neutrons are swapped. The bottom number, 56, is the proton count.
54 electrons would make Ba²⁺. A neutral atom has as many electrons as protons.

questions.stem: How many electrons are in the ion ⁷⁵₃₃As³⁻?
questions.exp: Electrons = Z - charge = 33 - (-3) = 36.
why: Subtracting 3 is for a positive ion. A 3- ion gained 3 electrons: 33 + 3 = 36.
33 is the count for a neutral arsenic atom. The 3- charge means 3 extra electrons.
42 is the neutron count (75 - 33), not the electron count.

questions.stem: Boron has two isotopes: boron-10 (20% abundance) and boron-11 (80%). What is boron's average atomic mass?
why: That is a plain average. Boron-11 is four times as common, so the average sits closer to 11.
The abundances are swapped: 0.80 × 10 + 0.20 × 11 = 10.20. Boron-11 is the 80% isotope.
That just adds the two mass numbers. Each mass must be multiplied by its abundance first.

questions.stem: Rhenium is 37.40% Re-185 and 62.60% Re-187. What is its average atomic mass?
why: That is the plain average of 185 and 187. Re-187 is more common, so the answer is above 186.
The abundances are swapped. Re-187 is the 62.60% isotope.
That is only the most common isotope. The average must include Re-185 too.

questions.stem: Why is the atomic mass on the periodic table a decimal?
options: It is rounded from the mass number
Each atom has a fractional neutron count
questions.exp: Elements are mixtures of isotopes, so the table lists a weighted average of their masses.
why: Electrons are nearly massless. The decimal comes from averaging isotopes.
The mass number is a whole count. The table value is a weighted average, not a rounding of it.
Every atom has a whole number of neutrons. Only the average across isotopes is fractional.

questions.stem: Which change would turn an atom into a different element?
questions.exp: The number of protons (atomic number) sets the element's identity.
why: That makes a different isotope of the same element.
That makes an ion of the same element.
Isotopes of one element have different mass numbers. Only the proton count sets the element.

questions.stem: Which observation led Thomson to his plum pudding model?
options: Alpha particles bounced off a metal foil
questions.exp: Thomson found that atoms give off electrons and reasoned that positive charge must balance them.
why: That was Rutherford's result, and it disproved the plum pudding model.
That was Bohr's idea, proposed after Thomson's model.
That was Chadwick's 1932 discovery of the neutron.

questions.stem: How does the modern (orbital) model of the atom differ from Bohr's model?
options: Electrons travel in fixed circular orbits
Electrons are scattered in positive charge
questions.exp: Orbitals are regions where an electron is likely to be (about 90% of the time); exact positions cannot be predicted.
why: That is Bohr's model, which the orbital model replaced.
That is Thomson's plum pudding model.
Electrons are always outside the nucleus; only protons and neutrons are inside.

questions.stem: What does an element's period (row) number tell you?
questions.exp: The period number equals the number of principal energy levels (electron shells).
why: That comes from the group (column) for representative elements.
That is the atomic number.
That is the mass number minus the atomic number.

sections.name: MCQ Set B: ions and formulas
tips: Read every choice, then cross off the ones you can prove wrong.
For particle questions write Z, A and the charge first: p = Z, n = A - Z, e = Z - charge.
For formulas, write both ion charges before you look at the choices, then check the sum is zero.
Distractors are built from real mistakes: a skipped subscript, swapped abundances, a reversed crossover. Name the mistake behind each wrong choice.

questions.stem: An ion with a 3+ charge contains 23 electrons. Which ion is it?
questions.exp: Protons = electrons + charge = 23 + 3 = 26, which is iron.
why: Vanadium has 23 protons, so V³⁺ has only 20 electrons. You matched the electron count to the atomic number.
Scandium has 21 protons, so Sc³⁺ has 18 electrons.
Calcium is in group 2 and forms 2+ ions, not 3+. It also has only 20 protons.

questions.stem: A compound has the formula XCl₂, and ion X contains 20 electrons. What is X?
questions.exp: Two Cl⁻ ions mean X is 2+. Protons = 20 + 2 = 22, which is titanium.
why: Calcium has 20 protons, so Ca²⁺ has 18 electrons, not 20.
XCl₂ needs a 2+ cation to balance two Cl⁻ ions. A 1+ ion would form XCl.
Chromium has 24 protons, so Cr²⁺ has 22 electrons.

questions.stem: An alkaline earth metal whose most stable ion has 36 electrons bonds with bromine. What is the formula?
questions.exp: Alkaline earth ions are 2+, so protons = 36 + 2 = 38: strontium. Sr²⁺ needs two Br⁻: SrBr₂.
why: Ca²⁺ has 18 electrons, not 36.
Rubidium is an alkali metal (group 1), not an alkaline earth metal.
Krypton is a noble gas; 36 is its electron count as a neutral atom.

questions.stem: What ionic compound forms when barium bonds with phosphorus?
questions.exp: Ba²⁺ and P³⁻: cross the charges to get Ba₃P₂, since 3(+2) + 2(-3) = 0.
why: The subscripts are on the wrong ions: 2(+2) + 3(-3) = -5, not zero.
Ba²⁺ and P³⁻ do not cancel one to one: +2 - 3 = -1.
3(+2) + (-3) = +3. Two phosphide ions are needed.

questions.stem: What ionic compound forms when aluminum bonds with sulfur?
questions.exp: Al³⁺ and S²⁻ cross over to Al₂S₃: 2(+3) + 3(-2) = 0.
why: The subscripts are reversed: 3(+3) + 2(-2) = +5.
Al³⁺ and S²⁻ do not cancel one to one: +3 - 2 = +1.
2(+3) + (-2) = +4. Three sulfide ions are needed.

questions.stem: Which element forms a 2- ion?
questions.exp: Selenium is in group 16 (oxygen family), which forms 2- ions.
why: Bromine is a halogen (group 17) and forms a 1- ion.
Arsenic is in group 15, which forms 3- ions.
Strontium is a metal in group 2 and forms a 2+ ion, not 2-.

questions.stem: Which series is NOT matched with the correct description?
options: Mg, Ca, Sr: alkaline earth metals
questions.exp: Boron, silicon and germanium are metalloids, on the staircase, not metals.
why: These are all in group 17, the halogens. This one is correct.
These are all in group 2. This one is correct.
These are all in groups 3 to 12. This one is correct.

questions.stem: When does a solid ionic compound such as NaCl conduct electricity?
options: As a solid at room temperature
Only after it is crushed to powder
Never, since the compound is neutral
questions.exp: Ionic compounds conduct electricity when melted or dissolved in water, because the ions can then move.
why: In the solid, the ions are locked in place and cannot move, so it does not conduct.
Powder is still a solid with locked ions, so it still does not conduct.
The compound is neutral overall but made of charged ions, which conduct once they can move.

questions.stem: What happens to a halogen atom when it forms its most common ion?
questions.exp: Halogens have 7 valence electrons, so each gains 1 to complete the octet and becomes a 1- anion.
why: Halogens are nonmetals with 7 valence electrons; they gain one to complete the octet, not lose one.
A halogen needs only one more electron to reach eight.
Gaining one electron is far easier than losing seven; halogens form 1- ions.

questions.stem: Which of these is a covalent compound?
questions.exp: Carbon and fluorine are both nonmetals, so they share electrons: a covalent compound.
why: Magnesium is a metal, so MgCl₂ is ionic.
Sodium is a metal, so Na₂S is ionic.
Lithium is a metal, so Li₃N is ionic.

questions.stem: What is the formula of calcium cyanide?
questions.exp: Ca²⁺ needs two CN⁻ ions. Parentheses keep each cyanide ion together: Ca(CN)₂.
why: Without parentheses the 2 applies only to N. Two whole CN⁻ ions are needed.
Ca²⁺ with one CN⁻ leaves a +1 charge.

questions.stem: Which ion has the same number of electrons as a neutral neon atom?
questions.exp: Neon has 10 electrons. Mg has 12 protons; losing 2 leaves 10.
why: Calcium has 20 protons, so Ca²⁺ has 18 electrons, like argon.
Chlorine has 17 protons, so Cl⁻ has 18 electrons.
Sulfur has 16 protons, so S²⁻ has 18 electrons.

questions.stem: What is the formula of sodium phosphate?
questions.exp: Phosphate is PO₄³⁻, so three Na⁺ balance it: Na₃PO₄.
why: Na⁺ and PO₄³⁻ do not cancel one to one: +1 - 3 = -2.
2(+1) + (-3) = -1. Three Na⁺ are needed.
That puts the 3 on phosphate. Sodium is the ion that needs three.

sections.name: MCQ Set C: molar mass and moles
tips: Read every choice, then cross off the ones you can prove wrong.
For particle questions write Z, A and the charge first: p = Z, n = A - Z, e = Z - charge.
For formulas, write both ion charges before you look at the choices, then check the sum is zero.
Distractors are built from real mistakes: a skipped subscript, swapped abundances, a reversed crossover. Name the mistake behind each wrong choice.

questions.stem: What is the molar mass of calcium cyanide, Ca(CN)₂?
why: That counts only one C and one N. The 2 outside the parentheses doubles both.
That doubles only N. The 2 applies to everything inside the parentheses.
That doubles calcium too. Only the CN inside the parentheses is doubled.

questions.stem: What is the molar mass of carbonic acid, H₂CO₃?
why: That counts only one hydrogen. The subscript 2 means two H.
That counts only one oxygen. The subscript 3 means three O.
That counts three hydrogens. The formula has two.

questions.stem: What is the molar mass of aluminum oxide, Al₂O₃?
why: That ignores both subscripts.
That counts only one aluminum. The formula has two.
That counts only one oxygen. The formula has three.

questions.stem: How many moles of MgCl₂ are in 45.8 g? (Molar mass 95.21 g/mol.)
questions.exp: 45.8 g ÷ 95.21 g/mol = 0.481 mol MgCl₂.
why: That divides the molar mass by the grams. Divide grams by molar mass.
That is the moles of Cl atoms, not of MgCl₂.
That halves the answer. Nothing in this step uses the subscript.

questions.stem: How many chlorine atoms are in 45.8 g of MgCl₂?
why: That skips the subscript: each MgCl₂ has 2 Cl atoms.
That stops at moles of Cl. Multiply by 6.022 × 10²³ to count atoms.
That multiplies by the molar mass instead of dividing by it.

questions.stem: How many hydrogen atoms are in 2.50 mol of methane, CH₄?
why: That counts molecules, not H atoms. Each CH₄ has 4 H.
That is the H count for 1 mol of CH₄, not 2.50 mol.
10.0 is the moles of H. Multiply by 6.022 × 10²³ to count atoms.

questions.stem: A sample holds 1.25 × 10²² formula units of Al₂S₃. How many aluminum atoms does it contain?
why: That is the number of formula units. Each has 2 Al atoms.
That uses sulfur's subscript (3). Aluminum's subscript is 2.
That counts all 5 atoms in each formula unit, not just aluminum.

questions.stem: How many atoms in total (P and Cl) are in 15.0 g of PCl₃?
why: That is the number of PCl₃ molecules. Each has 4 atoms.
That counts only chlorine atoms. Phosphorus adds one more per molecule.
That stops at moles of atoms. Multiply by 6.022 × 10²³.

questions.stem: A sample of SiO₂ contains 4.82 × 10²³ oxygen atoms. What is the sample's mass?
why: That skips dividing by 2: each SiO₂ has 2 O atoms.
That is the mass of the oxygen only, not the whole SiO₂.
That uses silicon's mass instead of the molar mass of SiO₂.

questions.stem: Which statement fits the law of constant composition?
options: Water's ratio depends on its source
A compound's ratio changes when heated
Water is always 2 H to 1 O
questions.exp: A compound always has the same elements bonded in the same ratio.
why: Every sample of a compound has the same ratio, wherever it comes from.
Heating can change state, but the compound's atom ratio stays the same.
Mixtures have variable composition. The law is about compounds.

questions.stem: What does one mole of any substance contain?
questions.exp: One mole = 6.022 × 10²³ particles (Avogadro's number).
why: A mole is a count of particles. Its mass is the molar mass, which differs by substance.
The mass of a mole depends on the substance (its molar mass).
A mole is a huge count: 6.022 × 10²³ particles.

questions.stem: What is the molar mass of sulfur hexafluoride, SF₆?
why: That ignores the subscript 6 on fluorine.
That puts the 6 on sulfur instead of fluorine.
That counts seven fluorines; the formula has six.

questions.stem: How many electrons are in the ion ⁷⁵₃₃As³⁻?
questions.exp: Electrons = Z - charge = 33 - (-3) = 36.
why: Subtracting 3 is for a positive ion. A 3- ion gained 3 electrons: 33 + 3 = 36.
33 is the count for a neutral arsenic atom. The 3- charge means 3 extra electrons.
42 is the neutron count (75 - 33), not the electron count.

questions.stem: Rhenium is 37.40% Re-185 and 62.60% Re-187. What is its average atomic mass?
why: That is the plain average of 185 and 187. Re-187 is more common, so the answer is above 186.
The abundances are swapped. Re-187 is the 62.60% isotope.
That is only the most common isotope. The average must include Re-185 too.

questions.stem: An ion with a 3+ charge contains 23 electrons. Which ion is it?
questions.exp: Protons = electrons + charge = 23 + 3 = 26, which is iron.
why: Vanadium has 23 protons, so V³⁺ has only 20 electrons. You matched the electron count to the atomic number.
Scandium has 21 protons, so Sc³⁺ has 18 electrons.
Calcium is in group 2 and forms 2+ ions, not 3+. It also has only 20 protons.

questions.stem: An alkaline earth metal whose most stable ion has 36 electrons bonds with bromine. What is the formula?
questions.exp: Alkaline earth ions are 2+, so protons = 36 + 2 = 38: strontium. Sr²⁺ needs two Br⁻: SrBr₂.
why: Ca²⁺ has 18 electrons, not 36.
Rubidium is an alkali metal (group 1), not an alkaline earth metal.
Krypton is a noble gas; 36 is its electron count as a neutral atom.

questions.stem: What ionic compound forms when barium bonds with phosphorus?
questions.exp: Ba²⁺ and P³⁻: cross the charges to get Ba₃P₂, since 3(+2) + 2(-3) = 0.
why: The subscripts are on the wrong ions: 2(+2) + 3(-3) = -5, not zero.
Ba²⁺ and P³⁻ do not cancel one to one: +2 - 3 = -1.
3(+2) + (-3) = +3. Two phosphide ions are needed.

why: These are all in group 17, the halogens. This one is correct.

questions.stem: Which ion has the same number of electrons as a neutral neon atom?
questions.exp: Neon has 10 electrons. Mg has 12 protons; losing 2 leaves 10.
why: Calcium has 20 protons, so Ca²⁺ has 18 electrons, like argon.
Chlorine has 17 protons, so Cl⁻ has 18 electrons.
Sulfur has 16 protons, so S²⁻ has 18 electrons.

questions.stem: What is the molar mass of calcium cyanide, Ca(CN)₂?
why: That counts only one C and one N. The 2 outside the parentheses doubles both.
That doubles only N. The 2 applies to everything inside the parentheses.
That doubles calcium too. Only the CN inside the parentheses is doubled.

questions.stem: How many chlorine atoms are in 45.8 g of MgCl₂?
why: That skips the subscript: each MgCl₂ has 2 Cl atoms.
That stops at moles of Cl. Multiply by 6.022 × 10²³ to count atoms.
That multiplies by the molar mass instead of dividing by it.

questions.stem: A sample of SiO₂ contains 4.82 × 10²³ oxygen atoms. What is the sample's mass?
why: That skips dividing by 2: each SiO₂ has 2 O atoms.
That is the mass of the oxygen only, not the whole SiO₂.
That uses silicon's mass instead of the molar mass of SiO₂.

questions.stem: What is the formula of calcium cyanide?
questions.exp: Ca²⁺ needs two CN⁻ ions. Parentheses keep each cyanide ion together: Ca(CN)₂.
why: Without parentheses the 2 applies only to N. Two whole CN⁻ ions are needed.
Ca²⁺ with one CN⁻ leaves a +1 charge.

parts.prompt: Why does an ionic bond form?
parts.model: A metal loses electrons to become a cation and a nonmetal gains them to become an anion, so both complete their octets. The opposite charges attract: that electrostatic force is the ionic bond.

parts.prompt: Why does the identity of an element depend on the number of protons it has?
parts.model: The number of protons is the atomic number, which sets the element. Electrons can be gained or lost (ions) and neutrons can vary (isotopes), but changing the protons makes a different element.

parts.prompt: Why is atomic mass on the periodic table a decimal?
parts.model: Elements exist as a mixture of isotopes. The table lists the average of their masses, weighted by each isotope's abundance, so it is usually not a whole number.

parts.prompt: Why do elements in the same group have similar chemical behavior?
parts.model: Elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons, and chemical behavior comes from the electrons, so they bond in similar ways.
